Optimal Market Making

Introduction¶

The market-making problem asks: given that you commit to quote firm bid and ask prices, how should those prices depend on your current inventory, the asset’s price dynamics, the arrival rate and price-sensitivity of client orders, your risk preferences, and the liquidity cost of closing your position? Chapter Market Making Fundamentals introduced the economic intuitions qualitatively. This chapter provides the mathematical answers.

We proceed in four stages. We begin with the classic market-microstructure models (Classic market-making models) — Grossman-Miller Grossman & Miller, 1988 and Glosten-Milgrom Glosten & Milgrom, 1985 — and derive their key results in full, treating them as static equilibrium benchmarks that characterize inventory risk and information-asymmetry spreads respectively. We then move to the single-trade model (The single-trade model): a dealer receives one RfQ, quotes a spread, and — if she wins — must liquidate the resulting inventory by end of day at market. This minimal dynamic problem captures all three spread components (static trade uncertainty, inventory risk, liquidity cost) in a single closed-form expression and extends cleanly to the multi-asset case via the covariance matrix of instrument prices.

The Avellaneda-Stoikov (AS) framework (Beyond a single trade: the Avellaneda-Stoikov framework) generalises to a continuous stream of orders: the dealer posts live bid and ask prices that attract arrivals from a Poisson process with exponentially decreasing intensity. We derive the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation in the general multi-asset setting, reducing the optimisation to a system of nonlinear ODEs for a scalar indifference function u(t,q)u(t, \mathbf{q})u(t,q), and show how the optimal quotes depend on the first- and second-order discrete derivatives of uuu with respect to inventory. Section Asymptotic approximations then develops the Guéant-Lehalle-Fernández-Tapia (GLF) infinite-horizon approximation Guéant et al., 2013, which linearises the system and yields closed-form expressions for the optimal spread and inventory-skew, making the parameter dependences explicit.

Section Applications to LOBs and RfQs discusses the application of the AS framework to both limit order books (the original context) and RfQ dealer markets. Finally, section Enriching Avellaneda-Stoikov collects four extensions that enrich the baseline model: a liquidity penalty that closes the loop with the single-trade model; Ornstein-Uhlenbeck mid-price dynamics that incorporate relative-value beliefs; asymmetric order flow (flow imbalance); and client segmentation as treated in the D2C context of chapter Modelling RfQs in Dealer to Client Markets.

Mathematical prerequisites are the stochastic calculus of chapter Stochastic Calculus (Itô’s lemma, Poisson processes) and the stochastic optimal control tools of chapter Stochastic Optimal Control (HJB equations, value functions).

Classic market-making models¶

Grossman-Miller: inventory risk¶

The model of Grossman & Miller (1988) isolates inventory risk in a stylised three-period setting. There are nnn identical market makers (MMs) and two waves of liquidity traders. At t=1t = 1t=1, a liquidity trader LT1_11​ needs to sell i>0i > 0i>0 units immediately. At t=2t = 2t=2, a second liquidity trader LT2_22​ needs to buy the same iii units. Time t=3t = 3t=3 is the terminal date at which all agents liquidate. MMs start at t=1t = 1t=1 with cash W0W_0W0​ and zero inventory. The asset price follows

S1=Sˉ,S3=S2+ε,ε∼N(0,σ2)S_1 = \bar{S}, \qquad S_3 = S_2 + \varepsilon, \quad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)S1​=Sˉ,S3​=S2​+ε,ε∼N(0,σ2)
(1)

where S2S_2S2​ is to be determined in equilibrium, and ε\varepsilonε is unknown at t=1t = 1t=1. All agents have exponential (CARA) utility U(W)=−e−γWU(W) = -e^{-\gamma W}U(W)=−e−γW with risk-aversion coefficient γ>0\gamma > 0γ>0.

Equilibrium at t=2t = 2t=2. When LT2_22​ arrives at t=2t = 2t=2, each MM holds i/ni/ni/n units purchased at t=1t = 1t=1. Each MM’s terminal wealth if she sells all her inventory at S2S_2S2​ is deterministic: W0+(S2−S1)⋅i/nW_0 + (S_2 - S_1) \cdot i/nW0​+(S2​−S1​)⋅i/n. If, instead, some inventory were carried to t=3t = 3t=3 at the risky price S3S_3S3​, the MM would demand a risk premium. In competitive equilibrium with symmetric MMs, LT2_22​ absorbs the full supply iii at price S2=S1S_2 = S_1S2​=S1​ — MMs sell at the same price they bought, earning zero on the round trip Grossman & Miller, 1988.

Equilibrium at t=1t = 1t=1. The MMs anticipate selling at S2=S1S_2 = S_1S2​=S1​ at t=2t = 2t=2, but S1S_1S1​ itself is the quantity to be determined. Each MM purchases q=i/nq = i/nq=i/n units at price S1=pbidS_1 = p_{\mathrm{bid}}S1​=pbid​. Her wealth at t=3t = 3t=3 if she unwinds at t=2t = 2t=2 is:

W=W0+(S2−pbid)⋅qW = W_0 + (S_2 - p_{\mathrm{bid}}) \cdot qW=W0​+(S2​−pbid​)⋅q
(2)

Since S2S_2S2​ is uncertain from the t=1t=1t=1 perspective (it depends on the new information arriving between t=1t = 1t=1 and t=2t = 2t=2, modelled as S2=Sˉ+ηS_2 = \bar{S} + \etaS2​=Sˉ+η with η∼N(0,σ2)\eta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)η∼N(0,σ2)), the MM faces price risk over the holding period. For CARA utility, the certainty equivalent of a normally distributed payoff X∼N(μ,σ2)X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)X∼N(μ,σ2) is

CE[X]=μ−γ2σ2\mathrm{CE}[X] = \mu - \frac{\gamma}{2}\sigma^2CE[X]=μ−2γ​σ2
(3)

The MM’s certainty equivalent of buying q=i/nq = i/nq=i/n units at pbidp_{\mathrm{bid}}pbid​ and selling them at the risky S2S_2S2​ is:

CE[W]=W0+(Sˉ−pbid)⋅in−γ2σ2⋅(in)2\mathrm{CE}[W] = W_0 + \bigl(\bar{S} - p_{\mathrm{bid}}\bigr) \cdot \frac{i}{n} - \frac{\gamma}{2}\sigma^2 \cdot \left(\frac{i}{n}\right)^2CE[W]=W0​+(Sˉ−pbid​)⋅ni​−2γ​σ2⋅(ni​)2
(4)

For the MM to be willing to absorb LT1_11​’s sale — i.e., CE[W]≥W0\mathrm{CE}[W] \geq W_0CE[W]≥W0​ — the bid price must satisfy

pbid≤Sˉ−γσ2⋅(i/n)1=Sˉ−iγσ2np_{\mathrm{bid}} \leq \bar{S} - \frac{\gamma\sigma^2 \cdot (i/n)}{1} = \bar{S} - \frac{i\gamma\sigma^2}{n}pbid​≤Sˉ−1γσ2⋅(i/n)​=Sˉ−niγσ2​
(5)

In competitive equilibrium, the bid is as large as possible consistent with MM participation, giving the Grossman-Miller spread:

pbid=Sˉ−i γ σ2n,spreadGM=2 i γ σ2n\boxed{p_{\mathrm{bid}} = \bar{S} - \frac{i\,\gamma\,\sigma^2}{n}, \qquad \text{spread}_{\mathrm{GM}} = 2\,\frac{i\,\gamma\,\sigma^2}{n}}pbid​=Sˉ−niγσ2​,spreadGM​=2niγσ2​​
(6)

The spread compensates the nnn MMs collectively for bearing inventory risk on iii units for one period. It increases with volatility σ2\sigma^2σ2, trade size iii, and risk aversion γ\gammaγ, and decreases with the number of competing MMs nnn — compression to zero as n→∞n \to \inftyn→∞ reflects perfect competition eliminating rents. Chapter Market Making Fundamentals (Market-making risks and trade-offs) presents the economic interpretation; the notebook notebooks/market_making.ipynb illustrates the parameter sensitivities.

Glosten-Milgrom: information asymmetry¶

The model of Glosten & Milgrom (1985) isolates adverse selection. A single competitive MM quotes firm bid bbb and ask aaa. The asset has a binary future value vvv:

v=VH with probability p,v=VL with probability 1−p,VH>VLv = V_H \text{ with probability } p, \qquad v = V_L \text{ with probability } 1-p, \quad V_H > V_Lv=VH​ with probability p,v=VL​ with probability 1−p,VH​>VL​
(7)

with prior mean μ=pVH+(1−p)VL\mu = p V_H + (1-p) V_Lμ=pVH​+(1−p)VL​. A fraction α∈[0,1]\alpha \in [0,1]α∈[0,1] of all counterparties are informed traders who know vvv; the remaining fraction 1−α1-\alpha1−α are uninformed liquidity traders who buy or sell with probability 12\frac{1}{2}21​ each, regardless of prices. Informed traders act optimally: they buy if v=VH>av = V_H > av=VH​>a, sell if v=VL<bv = V_L < bv=VL​<b, and do nothing otherwise.

Zero-profit ask. By Bayes’ theorem, the probability the counterparty is informed conditional on a buy order is:

P(informed∣buy)=αpαp+(1−α)/2P(\text{informed} \mid \text{buy}) = \frac{\alpha p}{\alpha p + (1-\alpha)/2}P(informed∣buy)=αp+(1−α)/2αp​
(8)

The MM’s expected profit on a buy is:

E[π∣buy]=a−E[v∣buy]\mathbb{E}[\pi \mid \text{buy}] = a - \mathbb{E}[v \mid \text{buy}]E[π∣buy]=a−E[v∣buy]
(9)
E[v∣buy]=αp VH+(1−α)/2 ⋅μαp+(1−α)/2\mathbb{E}[v \mid \text{buy}] = \frac{\alpha p\, V_H + (1-\alpha)/2\, \cdot \mu}{\alpha p + (1-\alpha)/2}E[v∣buy]=αp+(1−α)/2αpVH​+(1−α)/2⋅μ​
(10)

Setting E[π∣buy]=0\mathbb{E}[\pi \mid \text{buy}] = 0E[π∣buy]=0 gives the zero-profit ask. Analogously for the bid. For the symmetric case p=12p = \frac{1}{2}p=21​, so μ=VH+VL2\mu = \frac{V_H + V_L}{2}μ=2VH​+VL​​ and both informed buy/sell flows are equally likely, the expressions simplify:

E[v∣buy]=α/2⋅VH+(1−α)/2⋅μα/2+(1−α)/2=αVH+(1−α)μ=μ+α(VH−μ)\mathbb{E}[v \mid \text{buy}] = \frac{\alpha/2 \cdot V_H + (1-\alpha)/2 \cdot \mu}{\alpha/2 + (1-\alpha)/2} = \alpha V_H + (1-\alpha)\mu = \mu + \alpha(V_H - \mu)E[v∣buy]=α/2+(1−α)/2α/2⋅VH​+(1−α)/2⋅μ​=αVH​+(1−α)μ=μ+α(VH​−μ)
(11)

The Glosten-Milgrom quotes in the symmetric case are therefore:

a=μ+α(VH−μ),b=μ−α(μ−VL),spreadGL=α(VH−VL)\boxed{a = \mu + \alpha(V_H - \mu), \qquad b = \mu - \alpha(\mu - V_L), \qquad \text{spread}_{\mathrm{GL}} = \alpha(V_H - V_L)}a=μ+α(VH​−μ),b=μ−α(μ−VL​),spreadGL​=α(VH​−VL​)​
(12)

The spread is strictly proportional to α\alphaα — the fraction of informed flow — and to the magnitude of the informational asymmetry VH−VLV_H - V_LVH​−VL​. With α=0\alpha = 0α=0 (no informed traders), competitive pressure eliminates the spread entirely. As α→1\alpha \to 1α→1, the ask approaches VHV_HVH​ and the bid approaches VLV_LVL​: the MM refuses to quote inside the full range of possible values because any trade would be a loss.

In the general asymmetric case (p≠12p \neq \frac{1}{2}p=21​), the ask and bid shift asymmetrically around μ\muμ, but the qualitative message is identical: the spread compensates the MM for the expected loss on informed trades, funded by the expected gain on uninformed trades.

The single-trade model¶

Before tackling the full dynamic AS framework, we study the simplest non-trivial problem: a dealer receives one RfQ, quotes a half-spread δ\deltaδ, and — if she wins — must unwind the resulting inventory by the end of the day TTT. This model connects directly to chapter Modelling RfQs in Dealer to Client Markets but adds the explicit inventory liquidation and its market-impact cost.

Setup¶

The dealer holds an existing multi-asset inventory q0∈Rd\mathbf{q}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^dq0​∈Rd at time t0t_0t0​. A client sends an RfQ for instrument iii of size qˉ\bar{q}qˉ​ (e.g. a buy RfQ: the client wishes to buy qˉ\bar{q}qˉ​ units). The multi-asset mid-price vector St0=s0\mathbf{S}_{t_0} = \mathbf{s}_0St0​​=s0​ evolves as

dSt=Σ dWtd\mathbf{S}_t = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\, d\mathbf{W}_tdSt​=ΣdWt​
(13)

where Σ∈Rd×d\boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}Σ∈Rd×d and Wt\mathbf{W}_tWt​ is a ddd-dimensional Brownian motion, so ST−s0∼N(0, Γ(T−t0))\mathbf{S}_T - \mathbf{s}_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\, \boldsymbol{\Gamma}(T-t_0))ST​−s0​∼N(0,Γ(T−t0​)) with covariance matrix Γ=ΣΣT∈Rd×d\boldsymbol{\Gamma} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^T \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}Γ=ΣΣT∈Rd×d.

If the dealer wins the RfQ with half-spread δi\delta^iδi (she sells qˉ\bar{q}qˉ​ units at s0i+δis_0^i + \delta^is0i​+δi), her new inventory is q1=q0−qˉ ei\mathbf{q}_1 = \mathbf{q}_0 - \bar{q}\,\mathbf{e}_iq1​=q0​−qˉ​ei​. She then liquidates q1\mathbf{q}_1q1​ by time TTT at market, incurring a liquidity cost ℓ(q1)\ell(\mathbf{q}_1)ℓ(q1​) to account for the bid-offer spread and market impact of closing a position of that size. The client’s RfQ hit probability is f(δi)=e−kδif(\delta^i) = e^{-k\delta^i}f(δi)=e−kδi (exponential demand, as in chapter Modelling RfQs in Dealer to Client Markets).

Optimal spread¶

The dealer’s terminal wealth if she wins is:

WThit=qˉ(s0i+δi)−qˉ STi+q1⋅ST−ℓ(q1)W_T^{\mathrm{hit}} = \bar{q}(s_0^i + \delta^i) - \bar{q}\,S_T^i + \mathbf{q}_1 \cdot \mathbf{S}_T - \ell(\mathbf{q}_1)WThit​=qˉ​(s0i​+δi)−qˉ​STi​+q1​⋅ST​−ℓ(q1​)
(14)

The first two terms represent the transaction: she sells at s0i+δis_0^i + \delta^is0i​+δi and eventually buys back at STiS_T^iSTi​ (which equals s0is_0^is0i​ plus the Brownian increment). The third term is the mark-to-market of the residual position. Rearranging:

WThit=qˉ δi+q0⋅s0+q1⋅(ST−s0)−ℓ(q1)W_T^{\mathrm{hit}} = \bar{q}\,\delta^i + \mathbf{q}_0\cdot\mathbf{s}_0 + \mathbf{q}_1\cdot(\mathbf{S}_T - \mathbf{s}_0) - \ell(\mathbf{q}_1)WThit​=qˉ​δi+q0​⋅s0​+q1​⋅(ST​−s0​)−ℓ(q1​)
(15)

where q1⋅(ST−s0)∼N(0, τ q1TΓq1)\mathbf{q}_1 \cdot (\mathbf{S}_T - \mathbf{s}_0) \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\, \tau\, \mathbf{q}_1^T \boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{q}_1)q1​⋅(ST​−s0​)∼N(0,τq1T​Γq1​) with τ=T−t0\tau = T - t_0τ=T−t0​. Under CARA utility, the certainty equivalent is:

CE[WThit]=qˉ δi+q0⋅s0−ℓ(q1)−γτ2 q1TΓq1\mathrm{CE}[W_T^{\mathrm{hit}}] = \bar{q}\,\delta^i + \mathbf{q}_0\cdot\mathbf{s}_0 - \ell(\mathbf{q}_1) - \frac{\gamma\tau}{2}\,\mathbf{q}_1^T\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{q}_1CE[WThit​]=qˉ​δi+q0​⋅s0​−ℓ(q1​)−2γτ​q1T​Γq1​
(16)

The incremental gain from hitting the RfQ relative to not hitting (keeping inventory q0\mathbf{q}_0q0​) is:

ΔCE=qˉ δi−[ℓ(q1)−ℓ(q0)]⏟Δℓ−γτ2[q1TΓq1−q0TΓq0]⏟Δ(qTΓq)\Delta\mathrm{CE} = \bar{q}\,\delta^i - \underbrace{\bigl[\ell(\mathbf{q}_1) - \ell(\mathbf{q}_0)\bigr]}_{\Delta\ell} - \frac{\gamma\tau}{2}\underbrace{\bigl[\mathbf{q}_1^T\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{q}_1 - \mathbf{q}_0^T\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{q}_0\bigr]}_{\Delta(\mathbf{q}^T\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{q})}ΔCE=qˉ​δi−Δℓ[ℓ(q1​)−ℓ(q0​)]​​−2γτ​Δ(qTΓq)[q1T​Γq1​−q0T​Γq0​]​​
(17)

Expanding the quadratic difference Δ(qTΓq)\Delta(\mathbf{q}^T\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{q})Δ(qTΓq) with q1=q0−qˉei\mathbf{q}_1 = \mathbf{q}_0 - \bar{q}\mathbf{e}_iq1​=q0​−qˉ​ei​:

Δ(qTΓq)=−2qˉ (Γq0)i+qˉ2 Γii\Delta(\mathbf{q}^T\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{q}) = -2\bar{q}\,(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{q}_0)_i + \bar{q}^2\,\Gamma_{ii}Δ(qTΓq)=−2qˉ​(Γq0​)i​+qˉ​2Γii​
(18)

The dealer maximises expected utility: max⁡δif(δi) ΔCE\max_{\delta^i} f(\delta^i)\,\Delta\mathrm{CE}maxδi​f(δi)ΔCE. With f=e−kδif = e^{-k\delta^i}f=e−kδi, the first-order condition gives qˉ=k ΔCE\bar{q} = k\,\Delta\mathrm{CE}qˉ​=kΔCE, or equivalently:

δi∗=1k⏟static+Δℓqˉ⏟liquidity−γτ(Γq0)iqˉ⏟cross-hedge skew+γτ Γii2 qˉ⏟new risk\boxed{\delta^{i*} = \underbrace{\frac{1}{k}}_{\text{static}} + \underbrace{\frac{\Delta\ell}{\bar{q}}}_{\text{liquidity}} - \underbrace{\frac{\gamma\tau(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{q}_0)_i}{\bar{q}}}_{\text{cross-hedge skew}} + \underbrace{\frac{\gamma\tau\,\Gamma_{ii}}{2}\,\bar{q}}_{\text{new risk}}}δi∗=statick1​​​+liquidityqˉ​Δℓ​​​−cross-hedge skewqˉ​γτ(Γq0​)i​​​​+new risk2γτΓii​​qˉ​​​​
(19)

The third term carries a minus sign: when the existing inventory is positively correlated with instrument iii — meaning the new trade would add to risk — the cross-hedge term is positive and widens the spread; when the new trade reduces book risk it is negative, lowering the spread. This follows directly from the FOC qˉ=k ΔCE\bar{q} = k\,\Delta\mathrm{CE}qˉ​=kΔCE:

δi∗=1k+Δℓqˉ−γτ(Γq0)iqˉ+γτ Γii2 qˉ\delta^{i*} = \frac{1}{k} + \frac{\Delta\ell}{\bar{q}} - \frac{\gamma\tau(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{q}_0)_i}{\bar{q}} + \frac{\gamma\tau\,\Gamma_{ii}}{2}\,\bar{q}δi∗=k1​+qˉ​Δℓ​−qˉ​γτ(Γq0​)i​​+2γτΓii​​qˉ​
(20)

The four components have natural interpretations:

  1. Static uncertainty (1/k1/k1/k): even with zero price risk, the dealer incurs an option cost from the trade decision. The inverse of the demand elasticity kkk is the unit spread needed to achieve the optimal trade frequency. This term is independent of risk or liquidity costs.

  2. Liquidity cost (Δℓ/qˉ\Delta\ell / \bar{q}Δℓ/qˉ​): the per-unit cost of closing the new inventory q1\mathbf{q}_1q1​ at market, over and above the cost of closing the existing inventory q0\mathbf{q}_0q0​. For linear spread costs ℓ(q)=∑jℓj∣qj∣\ell(\mathbf{q}) = \sum_j \ell_j |q_j|ℓ(q)=∑j​ℓj​∣qj​∣, this becomes ±ℓi\pm\ell_i±ℓi​ per unit (adding to the position adds cost; reducing it may save cost).

  3. Cross-hedging skew (−γτ(Γq0)i/qˉ-\gamma\tau(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{q}_0)_i / \bar{q}−γτ(Γq0​)i​/qˉ​): if the existing inventory q0\mathbf{q}_0q0​ is positively correlated with instrument iii (and the new trade increases this exposure), the dealer demands a wider spread to compensate for incremental risk. If the new trade is a natural hedge against existing inventory, the spread narrows — the dealer offers a better price to reduce her book risk. This is the mathematical foundation for the inventory skew discussed qualitatively in chapter Market Making Fundamentals.

  4. New-position risk (γτ Γii qˉ/2\gamma\tau\,\Gamma_{ii}\,\bar{q}/2γτΓii​qˉ​/2): the pure inventory risk premium from holding qˉ\bar{q}qˉ​ units of instrument iii for the remaining horizon τ\tauτ, proportional to the instrument’s variance Γii\Gamma_{ii}Γii​, trade size qˉ\bar{q}qˉ​, and the dealer’s risk aversion γ\gammaγ.

Single-asset specialisation. For d=1d = 1d=1, q0=q0\mathbf{q}_0 = q_0q0​=q0​, Γ11=σ2\Gamma_{11} = \sigma^2Γ11​=σ2:

δ∗=1k+Δℓqˉ−γτσ2 q0qˉ+γτσ22 qˉ\delta^* = \frac{1}{k} + \frac{\Delta\ell}{\bar{q}} - \gamma\tau\sigma^2\,\frac{q_0}{\bar{q}} + \frac{\gamma\tau\sigma^2}{2}\,\bar{q}δ∗=k1​+qˉ​Δℓ​−γτσ2qˉ​q0​​+2γτσ2​qˉ​
(21)

When q0=0q_0 = 0q0​=0 (clean book), the formula reduces to the three-term result previewed in section Classic market-making models and consistent with case 2 of the RfQ pricing formula in chapter Modelling RfQs in Dealer to Client Markets. The q0q_0q0​-dependent skew term is the new ingredient: it shifts the entire quoted half-spread by −γτσ2q0/qˉ-\gamma\tau\sigma^2 q_0 / \bar{q}−γτσ2q0​/qˉ​, so a long existing inventory reduces the optimal half-spread on a sell-side RfQ (the dealer is willing to sell more cheaply to rebalance the book).

Beyond a single trade: the Avellaneda-Stoikov framework¶

The single-trade model fixes the quoting problem to a single event. In practice, a market maker faces a continuous stream of RfQs or limit-order-book arrivals, and her inventory qt\mathbf{q}_tqt​ changes continuously. The Avellaneda-Stoikov framework Avellaneda & Stoikov, 2008, extended by Guéant et al. (2013), provides the dynamic stochastic control solution to this problem.

Model setup¶

We work in the general ddd-asset setting. The state at time ttt is the triple (qt,St,Xt)(\mathbf{q}_t, \mathbf{S}_t, X_t)(qt​,St​,Xt​) where qt∈Rd\mathbf{q}_t \in \mathbb{R}^dqt​∈Rd is the inventory vector, St∈Rd\mathbf{S}_t \in \mathbb{R}^dSt​∈Rd is the mid-price vector, and Xt∈RX_t \in \mathbb{R}Xt​∈R is cash. The mid-price dynamics follow:

dSt=Σ dWt,Γ=ΣΣTd\mathbf{S}_t = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\, d\mathbf{W}_t, \qquad \boldsymbol{\Gamma} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^TdSt​=ΣdWt​,Γ=ΣΣT
(22)

For each instrument i=1,…,di = 1, \ldots, di=1,…,d, the market maker posts a bid half-spread δtb,i≥0\delta^{b,i}_t \geq 0δtb,i​≥0 and an ask half-spread δta,i≥0\delta^{a,i}_t \geq 0δta,i​≥0:

ptb,i=Sti−δtb,i(bid),pta,i=Sti+δta,i(ask)p^{b,i}_t = S^i_t - \delta^{b,i}_t \quad \text{(bid)}, \qquad p^{a,i}_t = S^i_t + \delta^{a,i}_t \quad \text{(ask)}ptb,i​=Sti​−δtb,i​(bid),pta,i​=Sti​+δta,i​(ask)
(23)

Client orders arrive as independent Poisson processes Ntb,iN^{b,i}_tNtb,i​ (buy orders for instrument iii, executed against the ask) and Nta,iN^{a,i}_tNta,i​ (sell orders, executed against the bid) with intensities:

λb,i(δb,i)=A e−kδb,i,λa,i(δa,i)=A e−kδa,i\lambda^{b,i}(\delta^{b,i}) = A\,e^{-k\delta^{b,i}}, \qquad \lambda^{a,i}(\delta^{a,i}) = A\,e^{-k\delta^{a,i}}λb,i(δb,i)=Ae−kδb,i,λa,i(δa,i)=Ae−kδa,i
(24)

The inventory and cash evolve according to:

dqti=dNtb,i−dNta,idq^i_t = dN^{b,i}_t - dN^{a,i}_tdqti​=dNtb,i​−dNta,i​
(25)
dXt=∑i=1d[(Sti+δta,i) dNtb,i−(Sti−δtb,i) dNta,i]dX_t = \sum_{i=1}^{d}\Bigl[(S^i_t + \delta^{a,i}_t)\,dN^{b,i}_t - (S^i_t - \delta^{b,i}_t)\,dN^{a,i}_t\Bigr]dXt​=i=1∑d​[(Sti​+δta,i​)dNtb,i​−(Sti​−δtb,i​)dNta,i​]
(26)

(Note: a client’s buy order goes against the market maker’s ask, adding to the MM’s cash and reducing her inventory.)

Objective and value function¶

The market maker maximises the expected CARA utility of terminal wealth including a quadratic inventory liquidation penalty ℓ(qT)=AT2∥qT∥2\ell(\mathbf{q}_T) = \frac{A_T}{2}\|\mathbf{q}_T\|^2ℓ(qT​)=2AT​​∥qT​∥2 (the cost of closing remaining inventory at market, generalising the single-trade penalty):

V(t,x)=sup⁡{δsb,i,δsa,i}t≤s≤TE[−e−γ(XT+qT⋅ST−ℓ(qT))]V(t, \mathbf{x}) = \sup_{\{\delta^{b,i}_s, \delta^{a,i}_s\}_{t \leq s \leq T}} \mathbb{E}\left[-e^{-\gamma\bigl(X_T + \mathbf{q}_T \cdot \mathbf{S}_T - \ell(\mathbf{q}_T)\bigr)}\right]V(t,x)={δsb,i​,δsa,i​}t≤s≤T​sup​E[−e−γ(XT​+qT​⋅ST​−ℓ(qT​))]
(27)

where x=(x,q,s)\mathbf{x} = (x, \mathbf{q}, \mathbf{s})x=(x,q,s) collects the state variables. The terminal mark-to-market XT+qT⋅STX_T + \mathbf{q}_T\cdot\mathbf{S}_TXT​+qT​⋅ST​ is the total portfolio value; the penalty ℓ(qT)\ell(\mathbf{q}_T)ℓ(qT​) accounts for the cost of liquidating any remaining inventory.

Ansatz and dimensionality reduction¶

The exponential utility and Gaussian mid-price dynamics suggest the change-of-variable ansatz:

V(t,x,q,s)=−e−γ(x+q⋅s+u(t,q))V(t, x, \mathbf{q}, \mathbf{s}) = -e^{-\gamma\bigl(x + \mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{s} + u(t, \mathbf{q})\bigr)}V(t,x,q,s)=−e−γ(x+q⋅s+u(t,q))
(28)

where u(t,q)u(t, \mathbf{q})u(t,q) is a scalar function of time and inventory only — independent of cash xxx (by the CARA structure) and of the mid-price s\mathbf{s}s (because mid-price changes enter wealth only through qT⋅ST\mathbf{q}_T\cdot\mathbf{S}_TqT​⋅ST​, which is already accounted for in the q⋅s\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{s}q⋅s term of the ansatz). The function u(t,q)u(t,\mathbf{q})u(t,q) is the indifference value adjustment: it measures how much the optimal pricing problem is worth relative to the mark-to-market of the current position.

The terminal condition on uuu follows from V(T,⋅)=−e−γ(⋅−ℓ(q))V(T, \cdot) = -e^{-\gamma(\cdot - \ell(\mathbf{q}))}V(T,⋅)=−e−γ(⋅−ℓ(q)):

u(T,q)=−ℓ(q)=−AT2∥q∥2u(T, \mathbf{q}) = -\ell(\mathbf{q}) = -\frac{A_T}{2}\|\mathbf{q}\|^2u(T,q)=−ℓ(q)=−2AT​​∥q∥2
(29)

The HJB equation¶

Substituting the ansatz into the HJB equation (see chapter Stochastic Optimal Control, The Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation), the multi-asset diffusion term gives:

12tr(ΣΣT∇s2V)=V⋅γ22 qTΓq\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{tr}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^T \nabla^2_\mathbf{s} V\bigr) = V\cdot\frac{\gamma^2}{2}\,\mathbf{q}^T\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{q}21​tr(ΣΣT∇s2​V)=V⋅2γ2​qTΓq
(30)

For each instrument iii, a bid arrival (buy order) transforms the state by x→x−(si−δb,i)x \to x - (s^i - \delta^{b,i})x→x−(si−δb,i) and qi→qi+1q^i \to q^i + 1qi→qi+1, so the change in VVV is:

V(t,x−(si−δb,i),q+ei,s)=V⋅e−γ(δb,i+Δi+u)V(t, x-(s^i-\delta^{b,i}), \mathbf{q}+\mathbf{e}_i, \mathbf{s}) = V \cdot e^{-\gamma\bigl(\delta^{b,i} + \Delta^+_i u\bigr)}V(t,x−(si−δb,i),q+ei​,s)=V⋅e−γ(δb,i+Δi+​u)
(31)

where Δi+u=u(t,q+ei)−u(t,q)\Delta^+_i u = u(t, \mathbf{q}+\mathbf{e}_i) - u(t, \mathbf{q})Δi+​u=u(t,q+ei​)−u(t,q) is the forward finite difference of uuu in dimension iii. Analogously, an ask arrival (sell order) produces:

V(t,x+(si+δa,i),q−ei,s)=V⋅e−γ(δa,i−Δi−u)V(t, x+(s^i+\delta^{a,i}), \mathbf{q}-\mathbf{e}_i, \mathbf{s}) = V \cdot e^{-\gamma\bigl(\delta^{a,i} - \Delta^-_i u\bigr)}V(t,x+(si+δa,i),q−ei​,s)=V⋅e−γ(δa,i−Δi−​u)
(32)

where Δi−u=u(t,q)−u(t,q−ei)\Delta^-_i u = u(t,\mathbf{q}) - u(t,\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{e}_i)Δi−​u=u(t,q)−u(t,q−ei​). Dividing the full HJB equation by VVV (which is negative), the equation for uuu is:

∂tu−γ2qTΓq+∑i=1d[max⁡δb,i Ae−kδb,ie−γ(δb,i+Δi+u)−1γ+max⁡δa,i Ae−kδa,ie−γ(δa,i−Δi−u)−1γ]=0\partial_t u - \frac{\gamma}{2}\mathbf{q}^T\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{q} + \sum_{i=1}^d \Bigl[\max_{\delta^{b,i}}\, A e^{-k\delta^{b,i}}\frac{e^{-\gamma(\delta^{b,i}+\Delta^+_i u)}-1}{\gamma} + \max_{\delta^{a,i}}\, A e^{-k\delta^{a,i}}\frac{e^{-\gamma(\delta^{a,i}-\Delta^-_i u)}-1}{\gamma}\Bigr] = 0∂t​u−2γ​qTΓq+i=1∑d​[δb,imax​Ae−kδb,iγe−γ(δb,i+Δi+​u)−1​+δa,imax​Ae−kδa,iγe−γ(δa,i−Δi−​u)−1​]=0
(33)

Optimal half-spreads¶

Each inner maximisation involves only one decision variable. For the bid side, we maximise over δb,i\delta^{b,i}δb,i:

max⁡δb,i  Ae−kδb,i[e−γ(δb,i+Δi+u)−1]\max_{\delta^{b,i}} \; A e^{-k\delta^{b,i}}\bigl[e^{-\gamma(\delta^{b,i}+\Delta^+_i u)}-1\bigr]δb,imax​Ae−kδb,i[e−γ(δb,i+Δi+​u)−1]
(34)

Taking the derivative and setting to zero yields a single equation. Defining Φb,i=δb,i+Δi+u\Phi^{b,i} = \delta^{b,i} + \Delta^+_i uΦb,i=δb,i+Δi+​u, the first-order condition is:

(k+γ) e−γΦb,i=k  ⟹  Φb,i=1γln⁡ ⁣(1+γk)(k+\gamma)\,e^{-\gamma \Phi^{b,i}} = k \implies \Phi^{b,i} = \frac{1}{\gamma}\ln\!\left(1+\frac{\gamma}{k}\right)(k+γ)e−γΦb,i=k⟹Φb,i=γ1​ln(1+kγ​)
(35)

Hence the optimal bid half-spread:

δb,i∗=1γln⁡ ⁣(1+γk)−Δi+u(t,q)\boxed{\delta^{b,i*} = \frac{1}{\gamma}\ln\!\left(1+\frac{\gamma}{k}\right) - \Delta^+_i u(t,\mathbf{q})}δb,i∗=γ1​ln(1+kγ​)−Δi+​u(t,q)​
(36)

An identical calculation for the ask side yields Φa,i=δa,i∗−Δi−u=1γln⁡(1+γ/k)\Phi^{a,i} = \delta^{a,i*} - \Delta^-_i u = \frac{1}{\gamma}\ln(1+\gamma/k)Φa,i=δa,i∗−Δi−​u=γ1​ln(1+γ/k), so:

δa,i∗=1γln⁡ ⁣(1+γk)+Δi−u(t,q)\boxed{\delta^{a,i*} = \frac{1}{\gamma}\ln\!\left(1+\frac{\gamma}{k}\right) + \Delta^-_i u(t,\mathbf{q})}δa,i∗=γ1​ln(1+kγ​)+Δi−​u(t,q)​
(37)

Defining the static half-spread η:=1γln⁡(1+γ/k)\eta := \frac{1}{\gamma}\ln(1+\gamma/k)η:=γ1​ln(1+γ/k), the optimal quotes on instrument iii are:

pb,i∗=Sti−δb,i∗=Sti−η+Δi+u,pa,i∗=Sti+δa,i∗=Sti+η+Δi−up^{b,i*} = S^i_t - \delta^{b,i*} = S^i_t - \eta + \Delta^+_i u, \qquad p^{a,i*} = S^i_t + \delta^{a,i*} = S^i_t + \eta + \Delta^-_i upb,i∗=Sti​−δb,i∗=Sti​−η+Δi+​u,pa,i∗=Sti​+δa,i∗=Sti​+η+Δi−​u
(38)

The reservation price for instrument iii is the mid-point of the optimal bid and ask:

rti:=pa,i∗+pb,i∗2=Sti+Δi−u+Δi+u2=Sti+u(t,q+ei)−u(t,q−ei)2r^i_t := \frac{p^{a,i*} + p^{b,i*}}{2} = S^i_t + \frac{\Delta^-_i u + \Delta^+_i u}{2} = S^i_t + \frac{u(t,\mathbf{q}+\mathbf{e}_i) - u(t,\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{e}_i)}{2}rti​:=2pa,i∗+pb,i∗​=Sti​+2Δi−​u+Δi+​u​=Sti​+2u(t,q+ei​)−u(t,q−ei​)​
(39)

The quoted spread for instrument iii:

pa,i∗−pb,i∗=2η+Δi−u−Δi+u=2η+[2u(t,q)−u(t,q+ei)−u(t,q−ei)]=2η−Δi2up^{a,i*} - p^{b,i*} = 2\eta + \Delta^-_i u - \Delta^+_i u = 2\eta + \bigl[2u(t,\mathbf{q}) - u(t,\mathbf{q}+\mathbf{e}_i) - u(t,\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{e}_i)\bigr] = 2\eta - \Delta^2_i upa,i∗−pb,i∗=2η+Δi−​u−Δi+​u=2η+[2u(t,q)−u(t,q+ei​)−u(t,q−ei​)]=2η−Δi2​u
(40)

where Δi2u\Delta^2_i uΔi2​u is the second discrete derivative of uuu in dimension iii. For a concave uuu (which is always the case here — the value function is concave in inventory due to risk aversion), Δi2u<0\Delta^2_i u < 0Δi2​u<0 and therefore 2η−Δi2u>2η2\eta - \Delta^2_i u > 2\eta2η−Δi2​u>2η: the spread exceeds its static minimum, with the excess reflecting the curvature of the inventory risk.

The equation for u(t,q)u(t,\mathbf{q})u(t,q)¶

Substituting the optimal half-spreads back into the HJB, and defining the constant c=A(1+γ/k)−k/γ/(k+γ)c = A(1+\gamma/k)^{-k/\gamma}/(k+\gamma)c=A(1+γ/k)−k/γ/(k+γ), the value function satisfies:

∂tu=γ2qTΓq+c∑i=1d[ekΔi+u+ekΔi−u]\partial_t u = \frac{\gamma}{2}\mathbf{q}^T\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{q} + c\sum_{i=1}^d \bigl[e^{k\Delta^+_i u} + e^{k\Delta^-_i u}\bigr]∂t​u=2γ​qTΓq+ci=1∑d​[ekΔi+​u+ekΔi−​u]
(41)

with terminal condition u(T,q)=−AT2∥q∥2u(T, \mathbf{q}) = -\frac{A_T}{2}\|\mathbf{q}\|^2u(T,q)=−2AT​​∥q∥2. This is a coupled system of nonlinear ODEs in time (one per inventory state q∈Zd\mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{Z}^dq∈Zd), where the coupling arises through the discrete differences in uuu. The system can be solved numerically by backward integration from TTT to t0t_0t0​, typically by truncating q\mathbf{q}q to a bounded grid ∣qi∣≤Qmax⁡|q^i| \leq Q_{\max}∣qi∣≤Qmax​.

For the single-asset case (d=1d = 1d=1), the equation for u(t,q)u(t, q)u(t,q) is:

∂tu(t,q)=γσ2q22+c[ek(u(t,q+1)−u(t,q))+ek(u(t,q)−u(t,q−1))]\partial_t u(t,q) = \frac{\gamma\sigma^2 q^2}{2} + c\bigl[e^{k(u(t,q+1)-u(t,q))} + e^{k(u(t,q)-u(t,q-1))}\bigr]∂t​u(t,q)=2γσ2q2​+c[ek(u(t,q+1)−u(t,q))+ek(u(t,q)−u(t,q−1))]
(42)

The left side drives the concavity: for large ∣q∣|q|∣q∣, the γσ2q2/2\gamma\sigma^2 q^2/2γσ2q2/2 term creates strong curvature in uuu that translates into wide spreads and aggressive skewing.

Asymptotic approximations¶

The nonlinear ODE system for uuu has no closed-form solution in general. Guéant et al. (2013) derive a tractable approximation valid for the infinite-horizon (stationary) problem, in which the horizon T→∞T \to \inftyT→∞ and u(t,q)u(t,\mathbf{q})u(t,q) converges to a time-independent function u∞(q)u^\infty(\mathbf{q})u∞(q).

The quadratic approximation¶

In the single-asset stationary problem, symmetry around q=0q = 0q=0 and the convexity structure of the ODE suggest the quadratic ansatz:

u∞(q)≈u0−θ2q2u^\infty(q) \approx u_0 - \frac{\theta}{2}q^2u∞(q)≈u0​−2θ​q2
(43)

for constants u0u_0u0​ and θ>0\theta > 0θ>0. The discrete differences under this ansatz are:

Δ+u=u∞(q+1)−u∞(q)=−θq−θ2,Δ−u=u∞(q)−u∞(q−1)=−θq+θ2\Delta^+u = u^\infty(q+1) - u^\infty(q) = -\theta q - \frac{\theta}{2}, \qquad \Delta^-u = u^\infty(q) - u^\infty(q-1) = -\theta q + \frac{\theta}{2}Δ+u=u∞(q+1)−u∞(q)=−θq−2θ​,Δ−u=u∞(q)−u∞(q−1)=−θq+2θ​
(44)

Reservation price. From the AS formula derived above, ri=Si+u(q+1)−u(q−1)2r^i = S^i + \frac{u(q+1)-u(q-1)}{2}ri=Si+2u(q+1)−u(q−1)​. Under the quadratic ansatz u∞(q)=u0−θ2q2u^\infty(q) = u_0 - \frac{\theta}{2}q^2u∞(q)=u0​−2θ​q2:

u(q+1)−u(q−1)=−θ2[(q+1)2−(q−1)2]=−θ2⋅4q=−2θqu(q+1) - u(q-1) = -\frac{\theta}{2}\bigl[(q+1)^2 - (q-1)^2\bigr] = -\frac{\theta}{2}\cdot 4q = -2\theta qu(q+1)−u(q−1)=−2θ​[(q+1)2−(q−1)2]=−2θ​⋅4q=−2θq
(45)

Therefore the reservation price and its skew:

r∞=S−θq,ψ∞=−θq\boxed{r^\infty = S - \theta q, \qquad \psi^\infty = -\theta q}r∞=S−θq,ψ∞=−θq​
(46)

The quoted bid and ask are symmetric around r∞r^\inftyr∞:

pa∗=r∞+η=S−θq+η,pb∗=r∞−η=S−θq−ηp^{a*} = r^\infty + \eta = S - \theta q + \eta, \qquad p^{b*} = r^\infty - \eta = S - \theta q - \etapa∗=r∞+η=S−θq+η,pb∗=r∞−η=S−θq−η
(47)

The spread is constant at 2η=2γln⁡(1+γ/k)2\eta = \frac{2}{\gamma}\ln(1+\gamma/k)2η=γ2​ln(1+γ/k), independent of inventory; the inventory effect appears entirely in the location of the bid-ask band.

Determining θ\thetaθ: the GLF result¶

Substituting the quadratic ansatz into the stationary HJB (∂tu=0\partial_t u = 0∂t​u=0) and expanding at leading order in qqq:

0=γσ2q22+2ccosh⁡(kθ/2)e−kqθ0 = \frac{\gamma\sigma^2 q^2}{2} + 2c\cosh(k\theta/2) e^{-kq\theta}0=2γσ2q2​+2ccosh(kθ/2)e−kqθ
(48)

This equation cannot hold for all qqq simultaneously with the quadratic approximation. The GLF approach instead matches the equation at q=0q = 0q=0 and uses a linearisation in θ\thetaθ (valid for small θ\thetaθ) to extract θ\thetaθ. The result of this procedure is:

θ=γσ22Ak−1(1+γ/k)k/γ+1\boxed{\theta = \frac{\gamma\sigma^2}{\sqrt{2Ak^{-1}(1+\gamma/k)^{k/\gamma+1}}}}θ=2Ak−1(1+γ/k)k/γ+1​γσ2​​
(49)

or equivalently, in terms of the characteristic spread η^=2η=2γln⁡(1+γ/k)\hat\eta = 2\eta = \frac{2}{\gamma}\ln(1+\gamma/k)η^​=2η=γ2​ln(1+γ/k):

θ=γσ212Aln⁡(1+γ/k)=γσ22Aη^γ\theta = \gamma\sigma^2\sqrt{\frac{1}{2A\ln(1+\gamma/k)}} = \frac{\gamma\sigma^2}{\sqrt{2A\hat\eta\gamma}}θ=γσ22Aln(1+γ/k)1​​=2Aη^​γ​γσ2​
(50)

The full optimal GLF quotes in the single-asset stationary case are therefore:

pa∗=S+η−θq,pb∗=S−η−θq\boxed{p^{a*} = S + \eta - \theta q, \qquad p^{b*} = S - \eta - \theta q}pa∗=S+η−θq,pb∗=S−η−θq​
(51)
spread∗=2η=2γln⁡ ⁣(1+γk),skew∗=−θq=−γσ22Aln⁡(1+γ/k) q\text{spread}^* = 2\eta = \frac{2}{\gamma}\ln\!\left(1+\frac{\gamma}{k}\right), \qquad \text{skew}^* = -\theta q = -\frac{\gamma\sigma^2}{\sqrt{2A\ln(1+\gamma/k)}}\,qspread∗=2η=γ2​ln(1+kγ​),skew∗=−θq=−2Aln(1+γ/k)​γσ2​q
(52)

Parameter dependences¶

The GLF formula makes the parameter dependences explicit and confirms the corrections introduced in chapter Market Making Fundamentals:

ComponentFormulaDepends on
Static spread2γln⁡(1+γ/k)\frac{2}{\gamma}\ln(1+\gamma/k)γ2​ln(1+γ/k)γ\gammaγ, kkk
Skew per unit inventoryθ=γσ22Aln⁡(1+γ/k)\theta = \frac{\gamma\sigma^2}{\sqrt{2A\ln(1+\gamma/k)}}θ=2Aln(1+γ/k)​γσ2​γ\gammaγ, σ2\sigma^2σ2, AAA, kkk

The skew sensitivity θ\thetaθ is not simply γσ2\gamma\sigma^2γσ2 — it also depends on the arrival rate AAA and the demand elasticity kkk. Higher order flow AAA reduces θ\thetaθ: a busy market maker can rebalance inventory quickly through trading, so she need not skew as aggressively for a given inventory imbalance. Higher demand elasticity kkk also reduces θ\thetaθ (more responsive clients means tighter necessary skew) but amplifies the static spread component.

Multi-asset generalisation¶

In the multi-asset stationary problem, the quadratic approximation takes the form u∞(q)=u0−12qTΘqu^\infty(\mathbf{q}) = u_0 - \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{q}^T\boldsymbol{\Theta}\mathbf{q}u∞(q)=u0​−21​qTΘq for a positive semi-definite matrix Θ∈Rd×d\boldsymbol{\Theta} \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}Θ∈Rd×d. The reservation price vector is:

r∞=S−Θq\mathbf{r}^\infty = \mathbf{S} - \boldsymbol{\Theta}\mathbf{q}r∞=S−Θq
(53)

so the skew in instrument iii depends on the full inventory vector through the off-diagonal elements of Θ\boldsymbol{\Theta}Θ:

ri,∞=Si−∑jΘij qjr^{i,\infty} = S^i - \sum_j \Theta_{ij}\,q^jri,∞=Si−j∑​Θij​qj
(54)

The matrix Θ\boldsymbol{\Theta}Θ is determined by the multi-asset analogue of the GLF equation, and its entries depend on Γ\boldsymbol{\Gamma}Γ, AAA, kkk, and γ\gammaγ. The key economic message is that correlated instruments share their inventory skew: being long in one instrument shifts the reservation price downward not only for that instrument but also for all positively correlated ones, reflecting the cross-hedging structure of the multi-asset covariance.

Applications to LOBs and RfQs¶

Limit order books¶

The AS framework was originally formulated for a market maker posting limit orders in a continuous limit order book Avellaneda & Stoikov, 2008. The original setting is the single-asset case (d=1d=1d=1) with the quoted mid-price following a zero-drift Brownian motion. The market maker maintains a bid and ask limit order and earns the spread whenever a market order arrives. The key assumption of exponential order arrival intensity λ(δ)=Ae−kδ\lambda(\delta) = Ae^{-k\delta}λ(δ)=Ae−kδ approximates the empirical observation that the book thins out exponentially as orders are placed farther from the best bid and offer.

In the LOB context, the “hold-to-horizon” framework with a terminal liquidation penalty is appropriate when the market maker takes a position at the start of the day and manages it until a hard close. Intraday, the inventory qtq_tqt​ fluctuates with each fill; the optimal quotes respond continuously via the finite-difference terms in uuu.

The GLF approximation is practically useful because it produces a simple real-time quoting formula: at any time ttt, compute the reservation price rt=St−θqtr_t = S_t - \theta q_trt​=St​−θqt​ (shifting the mid by the GLF skew) and quote bid rt−ηr_t - \etart​−η and ask rt+ηr_t + \etart​+η. The formula depends only on the current mid price, the current inventory, and the two pre-computed constants η\etaη and θ\thetaθ.

RfQ dealer markets¶

In dealer-to-client RfQ markets (chapter Modelling RfQs in Dealer to Client Markets), the single-trade model of The single-trade model is directly applicable as the unit decision. The stream of RfQs maps to repeated single-trade problems, where between RfQs the inventory evolves (from hedges and prior trades) and the remaining horizon τ=T−t\tau = T - tτ=T−t shrinks.

The connection between the single-trade formula and the AS framework is clearest in the serial approximation: treat each new RfQ as a fresh single-trade problem with the current inventory qtq_tqt​ and remaining horizon τt=T−t\tau_t = T - tτt​=T−t. The optimal spread is then:

δ∗(t,qt)=1k+Δℓqˉ−γτtσ2qtqˉ+γτtσ2qˉ2\delta^*(t, q_t) = \frac{1}{k} + \frac{\Delta\ell}{\bar{q}} - \frac{\gamma\tau_t\sigma^2 q_t}{\bar{q}} + \frac{\gamma\tau_t\sigma^2\bar{q}}{2}δ∗(t,qt​)=k1​+qˉ​Δℓ​−qˉ​γτt​σ2qt​​+2γτt​σ2qˉ​​
(55)

The third term −γτtσ2qt/qˉ-\gamma\tau_t\sigma^2 q_t/\bar{q}−γτt​σ2qt​/qˉ​ is the skew: it grows with the remaining horizon τt\tau_tτt​ (as in the AS finite-horizon formula) and shrinks toward zero at the end of the day as the urgency to rebalance the book increases. This formula can be used directly in a market-making system without solving the full HJB, at the cost of ignoring the interaction between the current RfQ and future arrivals.

Backtesting and performance comparison¶

Theoretical optimality guarantees are derived under the model’s own assumptions (Brownian mid-price, Poisson arrivals, CARA utility). To assess practical performance, Avellaneda & Stoikov (2008) propose a Monte Carlo back-test: simulate many independent trading days, record the terminal P&L after end-of-day liquidation, and compare strategies by the distribution of daily outcomes rather than by a single expected-utility number.

We implement three strategies under the baseline parameters (σ=2\sigma = 2σ=2, A=140A = 140A=140, k=1.5k = 1.5k=1.5, γ=0.1\gamma = 0.1γ=0.1, T=1T = 1T=1, S0=100S_0 = 100S0​=100):

  1. GLF stationary: quotes at rt=St−θqtr_t = S_t - \theta q_trt​=St​−θqt​ with constant half-spread η\etaη — the closed-form approximation derived above.

  2. Single-trade (EOD): at each step uses the finite-horizon formula derived in The single-trade model, with the current inventory and remaining horizon τt\tau_tτt​. The spread widens early in the day (large inventory-risk premium) and narrows to 2/k2/k2/k at close.

  3. Symmetric benchmark: fixed spread 2η2\eta2η around mid with no inventory management — a naive strategy that ignores the uuu-adjustment entirely.

A quadratic EOD liquidation penalty AliqqT2A_{\mathrm{liq}}q_T^2Aliq​qT2​ (with Aliq=1/(2k)A_{\mathrm{liq}} = 1/(2k)Aliq​=1/(2k)) accounts for the residual cost of crossing the market with any inventory remaining at close.

The notebook notebooks/market_making.ipynb also produces a third figure (mm_spread_dynamics.png) showing the intraday spread schedule: the GLF spread is constant while the single-trade spread narrows monotonically from wide in the morning to 2/k2/k2/k at close, and the skew (difference between ask and bid half-spreads) vanishes at end of day for the single-trade strategy regardless of the current inventory level.

Enriching Avellaneda-Stoikov¶

Liquidity: closing the position at market¶

The baseline AS framework with ℓ(qT)=AT2∥qT∥2\ell(\mathbf{q}_T) = \frac{A_T}{2}\|\mathbf{q}_T\|^2ℓ(qT​)=2AT​​∥qT​∥2 already introduces a liquidation cost at the terminal time. A natural extension for the dealer market is to allow partial liquidation throughout the day by trading at market with a spread cost.

Let δmkt\delta^{\mathrm{mkt}}δmkt be the half-spread the dealer pays to cross the market (hedge in the inter-dealer book). Then the dealer has a continuous control: in addition to choosing the customer half-spreads δb,i\delta^{b,i}δb,i and δa,i\delta^{a,i}δa,i, she can also execute a hedge of size vtiv^i_tvti​ at a cost of δmkt∣vti∣\delta^{\mathrm{mkt}}|v^i_t|δmkt∣vti​∣ per unit. The cash and inventory dynamics gain the hedging terms:

dXthedge=−∑i(Sti±δmkt)vti dt,dqti+=vti dtdX_t^{\mathrm{hedge}} = -\sum_i (S^i_t \pm \delta^{\mathrm{mkt}}) v^i_t \, dt, \qquad dq^i_t \mathrel{+}= v^i_t \, dtdXthedge​=−i∑​(Sti​±δmkt)vti​dt,dqti​+=vti​dt
(56)

In the HJB, the hedging control vt\mathbf{v}_tvt​ contributes an additional maximisation. For the quadratic penalty, the optimal hedge is:

vti∗=−1δmkt⋅∂qiu(t,qt)v^{i*}_t = -\frac{1}{\delta^{\mathrm{mkt}}} \cdot \partial_{q^i} u(t, \mathbf{q}_t)vti∗​=−δmkt1​⋅∂qi​u(t,qt​)
(57)

which drives inventory toward zero at a rate proportional to the indifference gradient divided by the hedging cost. When δmkt\delta^{\mathrm{mkt}}δmkt is small (liquid inter-dealer market), the dealer hedges aggressively; when it is large (illiquid hedge), she relies more on skewing client quotes.

The unified model — optimising jointly over client quotes δ\boldsymbol{\delta}δ and hedge trades v\mathbf{v}v — is the framework of Guéant (2017) and of chapter 10 of Cartea et al. (2015). The single-trade formula of The single-trade model corresponds to the limiting case v=0v = 0v=0 (no intraday hedging) with a one-shot terminal liquidation, i.e., AT=kδmkt/2A_T = k\delta^{\mathrm{mkt}}/2AT​=kδmkt/2.

Relative value: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck mid-price¶

The AS baseline assumes dSt=ΣdWtd\mathbf{S}_t = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}d\mathbf{W}_tdSt​=ΣdWt​ — mid prices are martingales with no drift. In spread products, pairs trading, or relative value strategies, the market maker may hold a mean-reverting view on the price. The natural model replaces the Brownian motion with a vector Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process:

dSt=κ(μ−St) dt+Σ dWtd\mathbf{S}_t = \boldsymbol{\kappa}(\boldsymbol{\mu} - \mathbf{S}_t)\,dt + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\,d\mathbf{W}_tdSt​=κ(μ−St​)dt+ΣdWt​
(58)

where κ∈Rd×d\boldsymbol{\kappa} \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}κ∈Rd×d is the mean-reversion matrix and μ∈Rd\boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^dμ∈Rd is the long-run mean.

The HJB equation acquires a drift term. With the same CARA ansatz V=−e−γ(x+q⋅s+u(t,q,s))V = -e^{-\gamma(x + \mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{s} + u(t,\mathbf{q},\mathbf{s}))}V=−e−γ(x+q⋅s+u(t,q,s)), the reservation price becomes state-dependent:

ri(t,q,s)=Si+∂qiu(t,q,s)r^i(t, \mathbf{q}, \mathbf{s}) = S^i + \partial_{q^i} u(t, \mathbf{q}, \mathbf{s})ri(t,q,s)=Si+∂qi​u(t,q,s)
(59)

The indifference function uuu now satisfies a PDE in both (t,q,s)(t, \mathbf{q}, \mathbf{s})(t,q,s) rather than just (t,q)(t, \mathbf{q})(t,q). In the single-asset OU case, the solution has the form Cartea et al., 2015:

u(t,q,s)=A(t)sq+B(t)q2+C(t)u(t, q, s) = A(t) s q + B(t) q^2 + C(t)u(t,q,s)=A(t)sq+B(t)q2+C(t)
(60)

where AAA, BBB, CCC satisfy a system of Riccati-type ODEs (see chapter Stochastic Optimal Control, Linear–Quadratic Stochastic Control). The reservation price becomes:

r(t,q,s)=s+A(t)q⋅∂s∂q+...=s+A(t)s+2B(t)qr(t, q, s) = s + A(t) q \cdot \frac{\partial s}{\partial q} + ... = s + A(t)s + 2B(t)qr(t,q,s)=s+A(t)q⋅∂q∂s​+...=s+A(t)s+2B(t)q
(61)

and includes a directional component A(t)sA(t) sA(t)s: when St>μS_t > \muSt​>μ (price above its mean), A(t)<0A(t) < 0A(t)<0 (for a mean-reverting process), so the reservation price shifts downward — the market maker expects the price to fall and quotes more aggressively on the sell side. This embeds a relative-value directional view into the quoting strategy without abandoning the optimal control framework.

Flow imbalance¶

In the baseline AS model, the arrival rates of buy and sell orders are symmetric: λb(δb)=λa(δa)=Ae−kδ\lambda^b(\delta^b) = \lambda^a(\delta^a) = Ae^{-k\delta}λb(δb)=λa(δa)=Ae−kδ. In practice, order flow is often imbalanced: the rate of customer buy orders AbA^bAb differs from the rate of sell orders AaA^aAa. This asymmetry may be persistent (a client base that predominantly sells, e.g., a corporate issuer hedging) or transient (intraday momentum in order flow).

Incorporating asymmetric intensities λb,i(δb)=Aibe−kδb\lambda^{b,i}(\delta^b) = A^b_i e^{-k\delta^b}λb,i(δb)=Aib​e−kδb and λa,i(δa)=Aiae−kδa\lambda^{a,i}(\delta^a) = A^a_i e^{-k\delta^a}λa,i(δa)=Aia​e−kδa modifies the HJB. After the same ansatz, the optimal half-spreads become:

δb,i∗=η−Δi+u,δa,i∗=η+Δi−u\delta^{b,i*} = \eta - \Delta^+_i u, \qquad \delta^{a,i*} = \eta + \Delta^-_i uδb,i∗=η−Δi+​u,δa,i∗=η+Δi−​u
(62)

where η\etaη is unchanged (only kkk and γ\gammaγ enter the static half-spread), but the equation for uuu picks up the asymmetry:

∂tu=γ2qTΓq+∑i[cib ekΔi+u+cia ekΔi−u]\partial_t u = \frac{\gamma}{2}\mathbf{q}^T\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{q} + \sum_i\bigl[c^b_i\,e^{k\Delta^+_i u} + c^a_i\,e^{k\Delta^-_i u}\bigr]∂t​u=2γ​qTΓq+i∑​[cib​ekΔi+​u+cia​ekΔi−​u]
(63)

where cib=Aib(1+γ/k)−k/γ/(k+γ)c^b_i = A^b_i(1+\gamma/k)^{-k/\gamma}/(k+\gamma)cib​=Aib​(1+γ/k)−k/γ/(k+γ) and cia=Aia(1+γ/k)−k/γ/(k+γ)c^a_i = A^a_i(1+\gamma/k)^{-k/\gamma}/(k+\gamma)cia​=Aia​(1+γ/k)−k/γ/(k+γ). When Aib≠AiaA^b_i \neq A^a_iAib​=Aia​, the stationary u∞(q)u^\infty(q)u∞(q) is no longer symmetric around q=0q = 0q=0, and the optimal reservation price shifts in the direction of the dominant flow even at zero inventory.

Concretely, if Aib>AiaA^b_i > A^a_iAib​>Aia​ (buy flow dominates), the market maker expects her inventory to drift negative (she sells more than she buys). The optimal response is to quote a slightly tighter ask (to attract the available buyers and prevent the drift from becoming too negative) and to widen the bid (since sellers are relatively rare). The flow imbalance thus introduces a flow-driven skew on top of the inventory-driven skew of the baseline model Cartea et al., 2015.

Client segmentation in dealer-to-client markets¶

In dealer-to-client markets, unlike anonymous LOBs, the identity of each counterparty is known at the time of quoting. This information is economically valuable: different clients have different price sensitivities kck_ckc​, different flow toxicities αc\alpha_cαc​ (the probability their trade is informationally motivated), and different average trade sizes qˉc\bar{q}_cqˉ​c​. The AS framework can be extended to exploit this structure Guéant & Manziuk, 2019.

The key extension replaces the single arrival process with a superposition of CCC client-class processes:

λcb,i(δb)=Ac e−kcδb,c=1,…,C\lambda^{b,i}_c(\delta^b) = A_c\,e^{-k_c\delta^b}, \qquad c = 1, \ldots, Cλcb,i​(δb)=Ac​e−kc​δb,c=1,…,C
(64)

Each client class ccc has its own parameters (Ac,kc)(A_c, k_c)(Ac​,kc​); the market maker observes the client identity before quoting and can therefore select a different spread δci\delta^i_cδci​ for each client. The optimal quote for client ccc is:

δci∗=1γcln⁡ ⁣(1+γckc)+Δi±u\delta^{i*}_c = \frac{1}{\gamma_c}\ln\!\left(1+\frac{\gamma_c}{k_c}\right) + \Delta^\pm_i uδci∗​=γc​1​ln(1+kc​γc​​)+Δi±​u
(65)

where γc\gamma_cγc​ is an effective risk-aversion coefficient that accounts for client toxicity: γc=γ+αc⋅kc\gamma_c = \gamma + \alpha_c \cdot k_cγc​=γ+αc​⋅kc​ (the more toxic the client, the higher the effective risk aversion of the market maker toward that client’s flow). The function uuu itself remains common across clients — it reflects the total inventory risk, not the risk from any single client — but the optimal static component of the spread is client-specific.

The practical implications are significant. A market maker dealing with a highly informed institutional client should quote wider spreads (γc\gamma_cγc​ large, so ηc=1γcln⁡(1+γc/kc)\eta_c = \frac{1}{\gamma_c}\ln(1+\gamma_c/k_c)ηc​=γc​1​ln(1+γc​/kc​) is wider) even when her current inventory is comfortable. Conversely, uninformed retail or corporate clients (αc≈0\alpha_c \approx 0αc​≈0) receive tighter spreads, and the market maker can be more aggressive in winning their business to rebalance the book. This framework provides the mathematical foundation for the client analytics component of the market-making system described in chapter Market Making Fundamentals (Components of a market-making system).

In the multi-asset, multi-client setting, the full model becomes computationally challenging. Guéant & Manziuk (2019) develop a deep reinforcement learning approach that parametrises the value function with a neural network and optimises over client quotes directly, enabling solution of market-making problems with dozens of instruments and hundreds of clients.
